Adults can sit A Levels at any age, and most now study outside a school timetable. How to do A Levels as an adult runs in one sequence: confirm what you need, choose subjects, pick a route, then secure an exam centre before paying anything.

Quick answer

  • No general upper age limit applies.
  • Study at a college, online, with a private tutor, or independently.
  • Outside a school or college, you enter as a private candidate and arrange your own centre place.
  • Coursework, speaking tests and practicals need extra arrangements, and not every centre offers them.
  • Providers and centres set their own requirements and fees.

Can You Do A Levels as an Adult?

Yes, and it is the same qualification. A Levels for adults come from the same exam boards, against the same specifications, as the ones 17 and 18-year-olds sit. No separate “adult A Level” exists.

Only the study method changes. Entry rules belong to the provider: some colleges recruit mature students, while some school sixth forms do not accept them. A Levels are classified as a Level 3 qualification in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, alongside AS Levels and the Access to Higher Education Diploma.

Decide Whether A Levels Are the Right Route for You

Start from the endpoint, not the subject list. What a university or employer accepts determines every decision after it.

  • University applicants: read the requirements for the specific degree and entry year.
  • Career changers: check what the employer, apprenticeship or professional body asks for.
  • Resit candidates: check whether the current specification differs from the one you studied.

Some adults need one A Level; others need several. Taking three because that is the school pattern buys qualifications nobody asked for. An Access to Higher Education Diploma, foundation year, BTEC Level 3, foundation degree or documented experience may be accepted instead: compare the alternative routes into UK higher education and confirm acceptance first, since an Access course may not substitute where a degree names a specific subject.

Decision checklist

  • Your final education or career goal
  • Whether a particular subject and grade are required, and how many A Levels
  • Whether alternative Level 3 qualifications or resits are accepted
  • Whether GCSE English, maths or science are required
  • Whether the subject includes practical work or non-exam assessment
  • Whether you need predicted grades and a UCAS reference

How to Do A Levels as an Adult

Eight steps, each depending on the answer to the one before.

Step 1 – Check Your University or Career Requirements

Requirements first, subjects second. For a degree, check:

  • required subjects, required grades, and how many A Levels
  • accepted subject combinations
  • GCSE requirements and resit policies
  • practical endorsement requirements
  • contextual admission policies
  • which alternative Level 3 qualifications count
  • whether qualifications completed in different years are accepted together

Read the whole course page on the university’s own site, and ask admissions in writing where anything is unclear. Requirements change between cycles, so check your entry year. Tariff points alone are not enough, because courses specify subjects and grades a UCAS Tariff total hides, though some degree routes with broader qualification criteria are more flexible.

Career changers check employer requirements, apprenticeship rules, professional-body registration, and any named subject or grade.

Step 2 – Choose Your Subjects and Number of A Levels

Choose subjects backwards from the requirement in Step 1, prioritising the named subject at the required grade. How many A Levels do adults need? As many as the destination asks for, which may be one. Taking one A Level as an adult is a complete application in many cases, though competitive courses may care about the combination.

Before enrolling, confirm:

  • the subject is available to private candidates, because not all specifications are
  • how it is assessed, since coursework and practicals change what you must arrange
  • that you have the prior knowledge: maths, sciences and languages assume solid GCSE foundations

New A Level or resit. Anyone resitting should find their previous results and certificates, then compare the current specification against the one they sat. Ask whether previous coursework marks can be carried forward, since not every component can be reused, and check the course’s resit policy.

Step 4 – Select an Exam Board and Specification

An A Level exam board writes the specification, sets the papers and issues the certificate: AQA, Pearson Edexcel, OCR, WJEC or Eduqas, and CCEA in Northern Ireland. Availability depends on the subject, your location and your centre, which enters candidates only for boards it is approved for. AQA guidance for private candidates and finding a centre for Edexcel examinations set out what each expects you to arrange.

Record six details together: exam board, qualification title, subject, specification code, assessment components and examination series. Textbooks and past papers must match that code, because materials for an older syllabus can cover different content.

Boards do not all assess a subject the same way, and the England, Wales and Northern Ireland versions can differ. Choose on availability and fit with your centre, never on a reputation for being easier.

Step 5 – Find an Exam Centre

This step decides whether the plan works, and it belongs before you pay for a course. A private candidate must be entered by an approved school, college or independent examination centre, because you cannot enter yourself.

Not every centre accepts private candidates. JCQ’s searchable list currently names around 190 that have confirmed they will, and advises confirming directly first. Get written confirmation that the centre:

  • accepts adult private candidates
  • offers your exam board, subject and specification
  • can run every written paper
  • can manage coursework or non-exam assessment
  • can arrange speaking assessments and practical endorsements
  • can support access arrangements

Then settle money and dates: an itemised fee quotation, the internal entry deadline, late-entry fees, and cancellation policies. Official guidance for private exam candidates and OCR information for independent candidates explain what a centre can and cannot do. Your course provider and exam centre are often separate organisations, so an online course does not automatically include exam entry.

Step 6 – Confirm Coursework, NEA and Practical Requirements

Some A Levels are assessed only by written papers. Others carry components a centre must supervise, and those decide which centres can take you at all.

  • Non-exam assessment (NEA): assessed work completed outside a written examination.
  • Coursework: a written or produced piece marked against the specification.
  • Practical endorsement: a separate pass or fail report on laboratory skills.
  • Speaking assessment: the spoken component in modern languages.
  • Portfolio assessment: submitted practical work, common in Art and Design.

Sciences, English, History, Geography, languages, Art and Design, Computer Science, Drama and Music all carry components beyond written papers, and the detail differs by board.

Ask who will supervise, authenticate and submit the work: an online tutor is not automatically authorised to authenticate coursework. The science practical endorsement is compulsory in Biology, Chemistry, Physics and Geology, reported as a separate pass or fail against the Common Practical Assessment Criteria. Confirm speaking arrangements for languages and portfolio requirements for Art and Design, and check the fee for each component.

Step 8 – Study, Register and Use Your Results

Create a study plan. Work backwards from the official timetable to weekly targets, scheduling separately:

  • new learning, revision and assignments
  • timed past papers, marked against official mark schemes
  • mock examinations, coursework and practical work
  • an error log, and contingency around work and family

Register for the exams. Enrolment and registration are separate acts. Confirm with the centre your legal name, date of birth, identification, board, subject, specification code, series, components, internal deadline, access arrangements and fees. Summer-series entry deadlines fall on 21 February, with late fees from 22 February, and centres set earlier internal deadlines. Check your statement of entry and keep every receipt.

Arrange access requirements. Contact the centre at the point of entry. Extra time, rest breaks, a reader, a scribe, a modified paper, a word processor or a separate room may be possible, but none is automatic: evidence is usually required, and the centre applies for you.

Sit the exams and receive results. Confirm the address, arrival time, permitted equipment and identification, then follow the rules on the day. Results come through the centre that entered you.

If a grade looks wrong, four services exist: access to scripts, a clerical re-check, a review of marking, and an appeal. A re-check completes within 10 calendar days of the request reaching the board, and an appeal follows only a review of marking. Deadlines fall in late September, and a review does not guarantee a higher grade.

Can You Study A Levels Online as an Adult?

The learning can happen entirely online. The examinations almost never do.

An online course typically provides recorded lessons, written modules, live tuition, tutor feedback, digital assignments and mocks. The final regulated examinations are sat in person at an approved centre, and your provider is often not that centre. Before paying, confirm in writing whether the package includes exam entry, centre fees, coursework support, practical endorsement, speaking assessment, predicted grades and a UCAS reference.

Use the official register to verify a regulated qualification. A provider’s completion certificate is not an A Level.

What Is an A Level Private Candidate?

A private candidate sits examinations at an approved centre without being enrolled there as a student. That centre may be a school, a college or an independent examination centre.

  • You: choose the qualification and specification, find a centre, meet its deadline, pay the fees, arrange any assessed work, and sit the papers.
  • The centre: makes the official entry, runs the examinations and agreed assessments, provides results, and processes post-results services.

No centre is obliged to accept every private candidate, and additional fees may apply.

Can You Take A Levels Without GCSEs?

There is no single rule covering every provider. Colleges set their own entry requirements, and some may enrol adults without formal GCSEs.

Knowledge is a separate question from paperwork. Maths, the sciences, languages and essay-based subjects assume a working GCSE-level foundation. Universities may also require GCSE English, maths or science in their own right. Functional Skills Level 2 is accepted by some in place of a GCSE, and not by others.

Check three things in order: what your A Level provider requires, what your university course requires, and what your career or professional body requires.

How to Apply to University With Adult A Levels

Adults apply through UCAS as independent applicants, without a school submitting on their behalf (UCAS guidance for applicants outside school). Enter completed qualifications exactly as awarded, and list anything still being studied as pending.

Pending A Levels usually need predicted grades, which is the practical problem private candidates hit. Ask your provider or tutor early whether they supply them; some UCAS-registered centres and online providers sell predicted grades and a reference, sometimes on the basis of mock examinations.

Your reference cannot come from family, a partner or a friend, and you cannot write it yourself. Suitable referees include a current tutor, a previous teacher, an employer or a professional supervisor (arrange an appropriate UCAS reference).

Mature applicants are read differently from school leavers, so show motivation, recent study, relevant experience and readiness for degree-level work. Check the current UCAS application and personal statement format, then complete the UCAS application process and compare universities supporting adult learners.

Compare which qualifications your intended degree accepts, and confirm the subjects, grades or credits needed in writing from admissions. Neither route is better in general, and course length is the weakest reason to choose between them.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  1. Choosing subjects before checking requirements. Confirm the requirement in writing first.
  2. Paying for a course before finding an exam centre. Secure the centre for your subject and board, then pay.
  3. Selecting the wrong exam board or specification. Write down the specification code and buy every resource against it.
  4. Ignoring coursework, NEA or practical requirements. Ask how each will be supervised and submitted before enrolling.
  5. Assuming the course fee includes examination entry. Request a quotation separating tuition, entry fees and centre charges.
  6. Taking more A Levels than necessary. Match the number to the requirement and put the spare time into the grade.
  7. Leaving predicted grades and the reference too late. Agree both at the start of the application cycle.
  8. Missing the centre’s entry deadline. Diary the internal deadline, not the board’s.

Adult A Level Planning Checklist

  • Goal, required subjects, grades and number of A Levels are confirmed.
  • Exam board and specification are selected and recorded.
  • A study route is chosen and an exam centre has accepted you.
  • Coursework, practical and speaking arrangements are confirmed.
  • Costs, deadlines and application timelines are realistic.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I take A Levels at any age?

Yes, though providers may set their own admission conditions.

Can I do A Levels without going to college?

Yes. Much of how to do A Levels as an adult happens outside a classroom: study online, with a tutor or alone, then enter through an approved centre.

Can I study A Levels online as an adult?

The teaching, yes. Final examinations are sat in person, and coursework, speaking tests and practical work need separate arrangements.

Can I take A Levels without GCSEs?

Sometimes. Provider requirements vary. You still need the underlying knowledge, and universities may require GCSEs separately.

Can I take only one A Level as an adult?

Yes. Individual A Levels can be taken alone. Whether one is enough depends on what your course or employer requires.

How do I book A Level exams privately?

Find an approved centre that accepts private candidates, confirm your board, subject, specification and assessment components, meet its deadline, and pay its fees.

Are A Levels or an Access course better for adults?

Neither is better in general. It depends on the degree you are aiming at, since some require specific A Level subjects. Confirm acceptance before enrolling.

Final Thoughts

Adults complete A Levels through colleges, online providers, private tutors and independent study, and the qualification is identical whichever route is taken. Choosing to study A Levels as an adult works when the sequence holds: check requirements, choose subjects, select a route, confirm the specification, find a centre, arrange assessments, then register.

Confirm your exam centre before paying any course provider, because the centre controls entry, components and deadlines. University applicants should get written confirmation from admissions.

Your next step is one email: ask an approved centre near you whether it accepts adult private candidates for your subject and board. To map the wider picture first, plan a UK education pathway or discuss your education options with an adviser.
